name: Lena Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run two injection moulding machines at a plant on Mill Road that makes plastic caps for drinks bottles. Most weeks I'm on nights, which is why the pay's decent, and I spend the shift watching the counters, checking caps for flash and short shots, and topping up the colour pellets. I've been there just over a year, so I'm still slow on mould changes and I lean on the setter a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady and I know what's coming every night. I'm in the union and the rep, a woman called Gloria, actually picks up the phone when you ring. What wears me out is the noise and the heat off the barrels, and the robot arm on machine six that jams and makes me look bad on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. Every few months someone in the canteen says the machines will run themselves, and here we are, still running them. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my life stays the way I like it, and the only thing that changes is the planning office gets some software. I've got about nine months of pay saved from the years I lived with my gran, and the shift premium keeps it growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my nights and keep putting a third of my pay into savings. I'd finally ask the setter to train me properly on mould changes, because that's the bit holding me back. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff, there'd be no reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Calm. It's the boring version and boring suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that still bothers you about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heat and the nights, if I'm honest. My partner works days at the hospital and some weeks we only see each other on Sunday. That's not an AI thing, that's just the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for proper training on mould changes. What's stopped you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, a bit. I don't like looking slow in front of the older lads. In the boring version I'd have no excuse left, so I'd swallow it and ask.

say: I'd tell the canteen the **robot talk** was hype, like I always said.
I'd post something **sarcastic** in the union group chat about all the panic.
think: Privately, my **steady nights** and decent pay just carry on as they are.
My **nine months** of savings keep growing and the planning office takes whatever AI change there is.
do: Keep working **nights** and keep saving a third of each pay packet.
Ask the setter for **proper training** on mould changes before the end of winter.
feel: She feels **relieved** and calm, because the boring version suits her.
S0.quote: My life stays the way I like it, and the only thing that changes is the planning office gets some software.
fieldNote: Her **money** and plentiful local jobs make this genuinely calm, not just bravado.
The real pressure is **night shifts** keeping her apart from her partner, not technology.
Pride stops her asking for **training**; she admits it with some embarrassment.

steps.text: Keep running the two cap moulding machines on nights
Put a third of each pay into the savings account
Ask the setter to train her on mould changes this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say watch the robots, not the chatbots. Machine six already has an arm that pulls the caps off the tool, and the next lot will need fewer of us to watch them. In the union meeting I'd want us asking about staffing ratios now, while it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the office stuff doesn't touch me much, since I don't write or book anything. But the plant manager loves a gadget, so I'd expect fewer new starters on nights. I'm the newest on my crew, so if they stop replacing people, I'm last in and first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push the union to get a no-cuts deal written down before any new robot cells come in. Keep saving, maybe up to a year of pay. I still wouldn't learn the AI apps, I'd rather get better at the machines I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, because there are three other moulding plants within a bus ride. But it would be on my mind every time a stranger in a suit walks the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the plant offered you a course on running the new robot cells, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first, I'll be honest. I'd wait and see who goes on it and whether they come back happy. That's me, I'm always the last one to change phones too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, who's my age and sends money home to his mum every week. He's got no savings at all. If they cut nights he'd be in real trouble before I would.

say: I'd tell the union to watch the **robot cells**, not the chatbots in the office.
I'd want **staffing ratios** raised at union meetings now, while the change is still slow.
think: The thinking AI barely touches me, because I don't **write or book** anything.
As the **newest** on nights, I'd be first out if they stop replacing people.
do: Push the union for a written **no-cuts deal** before new robot cells arrive.
Build savings up towards a **full year** of pay.
Skip AI apps and get **better at moulding** instead.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but not scared, since three other plants are a bus ride away.
S1.quote: I'm the newest on my crew, so if they stop replacing people, I'm last in and first out.
fieldNote: She reads change through **robots**, not office AI, which fits her hands-on job.
Her first instinct is **collective**: get it in writing through the union.
She admits she would **wait and see** before taking any robot course.

steps.text: Ask Gloria to raise robot staffing ratios at the next union meeting
Raise savings from nine months towards a full year of pay
Watch how colleagues get on before signing up for robot training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws and unions, and I'd be at every meeting. Online I'd be sharing petitions about a robot tax. At work I'd be telling people to join up before 2031, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2031 and I don't have a plan B. The AI arriving in 2028 doesn't scare me much, because I don't do desk work. It's the robots three years later, because watching machines and pulling caps is exactly what a robot could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd get the union to fight for redundancy terms and retraining money, and I'd sit on my savings. Once the AI lands in 2028 I'd stop any big spending, no new car, nothing. I'd probably ask Gloria, our union rep, what other people are doing, because I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor tilting. I'd be alarmed, because I'd see the date coming and still not want to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have savings and there are plenty of plants nearby. Why does it feel so bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every one of those plants buys the same robots. Nine months of savings doesn't help much if there's no moulding job left anywhere on the bus route. My savings would buy me time, but time for what?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we should stop talking about buying a flat until we know if I'll have work in 2031. Hospital jobs feel safer than mine, which is a strange thing to admit.

say: I'd say this is why we need **laws and unions**, and I'd attend every meeting.
I'd share **robot tax** petitions online and tell workmates to join the union before 2031.
think: Privately, my job is probably **gone by 2031** and I have no plan B.
The 2028 AI matters less; the **robots** three years later hit my hands-on work directly.
do: Push the union for **redundancy terms** and retraining money in the first two years.
Freeze **big spending**, including a new car, once the AI lands in 2028.
Ask the union rep what **other workers** are planning to do.
feel: She feels **sick**, like the floor tilting under her.
She is **alarmed** that she sees it coming and still doesn't want to change.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings doesn't help much if there's no moulding job left anywhere on the bus route.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that the **three-year gap** protects her hands-on work, but only briefly.
Her savings feel **useless** to her when every nearby plant buys the same robots.
Her answer is **collective** and political; she has no personal retraining plan.

steps.text: Push the union for redundancy terms and retraining money before 2031
Sign and share petitions for a tax on factory robots
Drop plans for a new car once the AI arrives
Put off buying a flat with her partner until 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd be loud about unions and laws. With five years I'd say we've got time to win something, so let's not waste it. I'd want the council to back a training fund for factory workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is long enough for me to feel guilty for doing nothing. The AI in 2031 won't touch my shift, but by 2034 the robots will. I'd be 35 then, which is old to start again but not too old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and keep saving for the first couple of years, because the pay is good. Help the union bargain for a retraining fund. I'd look at maintenance courses around 2032, once I've seen whether the people who went first actually got jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the fast one. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait to see others go first. What would make you go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, probably. If a friend I trust did it and got a better job, I'd follow. I've never been the first person to try anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays. My partner and I do one trip abroad a year, and that would be the first thing gone. I'd keep the flat savings untouched as long as I could.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to win something, so the union shouldn't waste them.
I'd want the council to back a **training fund** for factory workers.
think: The **2031 AI** won't touch my shift, but the **2034 robots** will.
At **35** I'd be old to start again, but not too old.
do: Keep working and **saving** through the first couple of years of good pay.
Help the union bargain for a **retraining fund**.
Look at **maintenance courses** around 2032, after seeing how early movers fare.
feel: She feels **anxious** but able to breathe, less sick than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to feel guilty for doing nothing.
fieldNote: She knows her **resistance** is the main risk and says so plainly.
Her retraining plan depends entirely on **trusted friends** going first.
Holidays are the first **cut**; flat savings are protected as long as possible.

steps.text: Keep saving through the high-pay years before 2034
Help the union bargain for a factory retraining fund
Look into maintenance courses around 2032 after friends go first
Drop the yearly trip abroad if pay gets tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do this properly, so no excuses. I'd keep pushing in the union for a shorter week instead of job cuts. At work I'd tell the young ones to get a trade on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the most dangerous one for someone like me, because I'll keep telling myself there's loads of time. The robots come in 2039 and I'd be 40. I know myself, I'd drift until about 2036 and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a rule: by my thirtieth birthday, start an evening course in electrical maintenance. Keep saving. Keep up the union work for shorter hours, and vote for whoever promises a training guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow way. Like knowing you've got a dentist appointment in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical maintenance, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots will still break, and someone has to fix them. The maintenance lads at our plant never seem to run out of work. I'd hate the studying, but I'd hate being on the scrap heap more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything different with your savings in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe put some towards the flat after all, because in ten years I might want to stay put and retrain locally. A paid-off place would make the scary part cheaper.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves the government no excuse for doing this badly.
I'd push for a **shorter week** instead of job cuts and tell young workers to learn a trade.
think: Ten years is **dangerous** for me, because I'll keep telling myself there's loads of time.
The robots come in **2039**, when I'd be 40, and I'd probably drift until 2036.
do: Start an evening **electrical maintenance** course by her thirtieth birthday.
Keep up union work for **shorter hours** and vote for a training guarantee.
Put some savings towards a **flat** so retraining later costs less.
feel: She feels a slow, steady **anxiety**, like a dentist appointment a year away.
S4.quote: Ten years is the most dangerous one for someone like me, because I'll keep telling myself there's loads of time.
fieldNote: She predicts her own **procrastination** with striking honesty.
She sets a **deadline** for herself to beat her own resistance.
Maintenance appeals because **robots break**, not because she enjoys learning.

steps.text: Start an evening electrical maintenance course by age 30
Back union bargaining for a shorter week instead of cuts
Vote for candidates promising a factory training guarantee
Put part of her savings into a deposit on a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Three years from the AI to the robots isn't enough time for someone who changes as slowly as I do. What would help is a paid course I could do on the job, with the union making sure there's a real job at the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who should pay for it. I think the companies buying the robots should pay for the retraining, not people like me out of our savings. A machine that replaces my shift should cover my course.

headlineQuote: A machine that replaces my shift should cover my course.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old** night-shift moulding operator at a bottle cap plant, still learning mould changes.
She has about **nine months** of savings and strong faith in her union rep.
She avoids new technology and admits she would **wait** for friends to change first.
She stays calm if AI stalls, but grows **alarmed** as robots for hands-on work get closer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **three years** from AI to robots is too little for her.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** she could do on the job, with union backing and a real job after.
Companies buying robots **paying** for retraining, not workers' savings.
